thread:
Sam L: Quick follow-up from last week's shim RFC — we still haven't nailed down how auth headers should be propagated when a request routes hosted -> dedicated -> private as a fallback. Also need to be explicit about which rate-limit buckets apply at each hop. Anyone free for a short sync?
Lia P: +1, this popped up in my tests yesterday. The private sidecar dropped X-Client-ID once we rewrote headers.
Omar R: Can you paste the trace? I want to see where the header was mutated.
Lia P: sure, here's the condensed flow: hosted proxy -> dedicated router -> private sidecar. In the dedicated router we add `X-Redwood-Tenant` and rewrite `Authorization` to `Bearer <token>`. The private sidecar expects `X-Client-ID` and `Authorization` unchanged, so it rejected and fell back to anonymous path.
Kevin M: That's the crux — we have three overlapping responsibilities: identity propagation (headers), tenant scoping (tenant header), and quota enforcement (rate buckets). We should document a deterministic order for mutations and which component owns which header.
Sam L: Proposal: immutable identity headers (e.g., Authorization, X-Client-ID) must be forwarded unchanged. Anything we set for routing (X-Redwood-Tenant, X-Routing-Stage) is additive. If a component must transform identity, it must emit `X-Identity-Orig` and `X-Identity-Transformed` and trigger an audit event. Thoughts?
Omar R: I like the audit bit. Also we need a concrete rate-limit resolution rule. Right now, hosted enforces per-api-key, dedicated enforces per-tenant, private enforces per-deployment. Which one wins when they disagree?
Lia P: in practice hosted often has stricter burst limits, so downstream gets 429 first. That made a client think the private deployment was rate-limited.
Kevin M: Suggestion: rate-limit precedence matrix: 1) local enforcement wins for immediate capacity (private), 2) if local allows but upstream denies, propagate the upstream decision as a 429 with `X-Rate-Limit-Origin`. If upstream rejects, we should not silently accept downstream requests.
Sam L: Draft matrix:
```
# Rule matrix (pseudo)
if private.denies: return 429 (origin=private)
else if dedicated.denies: return 429 (origin=dedicated)
else if hosted.denies: return 429 (origin=hosted)
else proceed
```
Lia P: That seems reasonable. We need a fallback behavior for when a middleware times out checking an upstream bucket — return 503 or assume allowed?
Omar R: Fail-closed for auth, fail-open for rate checks? Meh, dangerous. I'd prefer fail-closed only for authorization. For rate checks, default to allowing but mark request with `X-Rate-Check-Error` and emit a metric.
Kevin M: Agree with Omar. Operationally we can tail drop if we detect backpressure but shouldn't block.
Sam L: OK: consolidate into two policies: auth policy = fail-closed; rate policy = fail-open with observability tag and metric. Also enforce header immutability for identity headers, with explicit transformation protocol.
arch-bot: deploy-bot: small note — can we avoid header name collisions with cloud LB? I've seen rewrite rules upstream. Suggest prefix `X-RW-` for internal wire headers (e.g., `X-RW-Tenant`, `X-RW-Identity-Orig`).
Lia P: +1 to `X-RW-` prefix. Also we should list the canonical set in our adapter manifest so adapters can validate.
Omar R: I'll draft a compatibility matrix (CSV) with columns: header, owner, mutability, audit_required, example. Will post a PR.
Kevin M: I'll add unit tests to the dedicated router that assert header passthrough and the rate-limit precedence. I'll also add an integration test harness that flips behavior flags.
Sam L: Great. Next steps: Omar to open PR with matrix, Kevin adds tests, Lia to run integration smoke. We reconvene once PR is up. Thanks all. :thumbsup:
